F-001.title: Kafka decode failures are silently dropped: no DLT, no retry, no operator visibility
F-001.actual: BaseKafkaConsumer.decodeContained() catches every decode exception, logs at ERROR and returns null; the caller then returns without invoking the handler, so the record is ack-skipped. A handler exception, by contrast, DOES propagate to the container error handler (DefaultErrorHandler + DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, FixedBackOff(1000ms, 3 retries)). KafkaProperties.Retry (backoff-ms, max-attempts) is documented 'INTENTIONALLY UNUSED' - the real retry policy is hardcoded in BaseKafkaListenerConfig.
F-001.expected: A malformed or poison record must be routed to the DLQ (or at minimum surfaced as a metric) rather than dropped, so the loss is observable and replayable.
F-001.trigger: Any payload that does not bind to the target DTO - schema drift, a producer bug, or corruption.
F-001.root_cause: Deliberate 'ack-always poison posture' in the decode path, plus a dead Retry configuration block that operators can tune without effect.
F-001.consequences: Silent loss of order / payment / shipping / rating / media events. The offset advances as if the event had been handled; no DLQ entry exists; only a log line records it. A schema-evolution mistake upstream can therefore drop events across the fleet with no alarm.
F-001.remediation: Make the decode failure path publish to the DLQ (or throw so the container error handler routes it), and either wire shop.kafka.retry into BaseKafkaListenerConfig or delete the dead block.
F-001.regression_test: Unit test: a consumer given a malformed payload must either publish to the DLT topic or raise the error so the container routes it; the offset must not advance as a silent success.

F-002.title: Four published lifecycle topics have no consumer: inventory, promotion, category, brand
F-002.actual: Producers publish shop.inventory.events.v1, shop.promotion.lifecycle.v1, shop.category.lifecycle.v1 and shop.brand.lifecycle.v1. A fleet-wide scan for @KafkaListener shows no consumer bound to any of these four topics.
F-002.expected: Every published lifecycle topic either has a consumer or is explicitly documented as fire-and-forget audit.
F-002.root_cause: Topics declared by producers without a matching consumer contract.
F-002.consequences: Published events accumulate with no consumer; documentation implies downstream projections that do not exist.
F-002.remediation: Document the four topics as unconsumed, or implement the missing projections (for example category/brand into the search index).
F-002.regression_test: Static topology test: every produced topic must have a declared consumer or an explicit allow-list entry.

F-010.title: Stock columns have no non-negative invariant: reserved_quantity/available_quantity can go negative
F-010.actual: changelog-001 creates inventory.available_quantity and inventory.reserved_quantity as plain INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 with no CHECK constraint. InventoryServiceImpl.commit() performs inventory.setReservedQuantity(reserved - q) and setAvailableQuantity(available - q) with no floor; release() does the same for reservedQuantity. The expiry sweep clamps with Math.max(0, ...) but the service path does not. The JPA @Version column only detects concurrent modification, it does not prevent a negative value.
F-010.expected: Stock cannot become incorrectly negative - enforced in the database as the last line of defence, and clamped in the application.
F-010.trigger: A commit or release that runs after the expiry sweep already returned the hold (sweep commits first, commit() then subtracts from an already-decremented reserved_quantity), or any arithmetic drift between the reserve/commit/release paths.
F-010.root_cause: Invariant expressed only in application arithmetic with an inconsistent clamp; no declarative constraint at the storage layer.
F-010.consequences: Negative stock counters corrupt the capacity guard (available - reserved >= qty) so subsequent reservations can oversell; the overselling is silent because no check rejects the write.
F-010.remediation: Add CHECK (available_quantity >= 0) and CHECK (reserved_quantity >= 0) via a new Liquibase changeset, and clamp the service-side arithmetic with Math.max(0, ...).
F-010.regression_test: Concurrency test: N concurrent commits of the same reservation plus a concurrent expiry sweep must leave reserved_quantity >= 0 and available_quantity >= 0; a direct negative write must be rejected by the DB.

F-010.remediation_applied: New Liquibase changeset inventory-service/changelog-004 adds CHECK (available_quantity >= 0) and CHECK (reserved_quantity >= 0) as NOT VALID (enforced for new/updated rows, no table lock, no failure on legacy rows). InventoryServiceImpl.commit() and release() now reject an arithmetic outcome that would go negative with BusinessException STOCK_INSUFFICIENT instead of writing it. The atomic reserve/release statements guard the same invariant in SQL.

F-011.title: Reservation row has no version column: the expiry sweep can overwrite a COMMITTED reservation with EXPIRED (lost update) and double-decrement stock
F-011.actual: Reservation has no @Version field and the reservations table has no version column. ReservationCleanupScheduler.releaseAllExpiredReservations() selects expired PENDING rows with an unlocked SELECT (findByStatusAndExpiresAtBefore) and then calls reservationRepository.saveAll(reservations) after mutating them to EXPIRED. InventoryServiceImpl.commit() loads the same row without a lock and writes status=COMMITTED. Whichever transaction commits last wins.
F-011.expected: A reservation that has been committed must never be reverted to EXPIRED, and a committed reservation's stock must be released exactly once.
F-011.trigger: A commit() that starts just before the reservation TTL elapses, racing with the 60-second expiry sweep.
F-011.root_cause: No optimistic-locking or pessimistic-locking discipline on the reservation aggregate, and the sweep performs a blind read-modify-write.
F-011.consequences: A paid and confirmed order's reservation is marked EXPIRED; the release path then treats it as already terminalized and never restores or correctly accounts for the stock, producing stock inflation and overselling. The reservation can also be released twice against the inventory counters.
F-011.remediation: Add a version column to reservations (Liquibase changeset) with @Version on the entity, and make the sweep claim rows with a locking/conditional UPDATE (status = PENDING AND expires_at < now) so only one writer can transition the row.
F-011.regression_test: Concurrency test: commit() and the expiry sweep racing on the same reservation must end with exactly one terminal status and a single stock movement.

history.note: inventory-service: new unit tests sweep_claimsExpiredRowsAndReleasesReservedQuantity, sweep_skipsRowsAlreadyClaimedByAnotherWriter (the F-011 lost-update regression), sweep_publishesReleasedEventForEa
inventory-service 64/64 green; sweep_skipsRowsAlreadyClaimedByAnotherWriter asserts the lost-update regression (a claim that affects zero rows must NOT move stock).

F-011.remediation_applied: New Liquibase changeset adds reservations.version BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 and the Reservation entity gains @Version. The expiry sweep no longer performs an unlocked SELECT + blind save: it CLAIMS each row with a conditional UPDATE (status = PENDING -> EXPIRED, version + 1) and only moves stock for the rows it actually claimed. The inventory decrement is an atomic guarded UPDATE (reservedQuantity >= qty) that can never over-credit.
F-011.verification_evidence: inventory-service 64/64 green; sweep_skipsRowsAlreadyClaimedByAnotherWriter asserts the lost-update regression (a claim that affects zero rows must NOT move stock).

F-012.title: Expiry sweep releases stock without emitting the inventory.released.v1 event - outbox and domain state diverge
F-012.actual: InventoryServiceImpl.release() calls publisher.publishReleased(inventory, r, "PENDING") and releaseCommitted() calls publishReleased(inv, r, "COMMITTED"), both writing an outbox row in the same transaction. ReservationCleanupScheduler.releaseBatch() decrements reservedQuantity and flips the status to EXPIRED but never calls the event publisher, so no outbox row is written.
F-012.expected: Every stock movement - including TTL expiry - produces the corresponding lifecycle event in the same transaction.
F-012.trigger: Any reservation that reaches its TTL and is swept.
F-012.root_cause: The scheduler reimplements the release transition instead of delegating to the shared transactional release path.
F-012.consequences: shop.inventory.events.v1 under-reports releases; any downstream projection (or reconciliation job) that trusts the event stream diverges from the inventory table. It also hides the release from the outbox-driven audit trail.
F-012.remediation: Route the sweep through the same transactional release path so the outbox row is written atomically with the stock change.
F-012.regression_test: Integration test: sweeping an expired reservation must leave exactly one outbox row of type inventory.released.v1 with previousStatus=PENDING.

F-012.remediation_applied: ReservationCleanupScheduler now publishes an inventory.released.v1 outbox row (previousStatus=PENDING) for every expired reservation it claims, in the same transaction as the stock movement.

F-013.title: Outbox relay holds a PESSIMISTIC_WRITE row lock and an open DB transaction across a blocking Kafka publish
F-013.actual: InventoryOutboxRelay.relay() wraps claimOnePending (PESSIMISTIC_WRITE + SKIP LOCKED), the blocking kafkaPublisher.publish() call (future.get(10s)) and the status save in a single TransactionTemplate transaction. The row lock and the DB transaction therefore stay open for the full broker round-trip, up to 10 seconds per event, with a batch size of 100.
F-013.expected: The claim transaction is short; the Kafka publish happens outside the lock; the mark-published step is its own transaction.
F-013.trigger: A slow or degraded Kafka broker.
F-013.root_cause: Claim, publish and mark-published were fused into one transaction to prevent double-publish, trading lock-hold time for correctness.
F-013.consequences: Long-running transactions hold row locks and connections; under broker degradation the relay can pin a HikariCP connection for 10s per event and exhaust the pool (default maximum-pool-size=20), and the outbox_events table accumulates PENDING rows behind head-of-line blocking.
F-013.remediation: Split into three phases: (1) short claim transaction that flips the row to SENDING and returns it; (2) publish outside any transaction; (3) short update transaction that sets SENT/FAILED. Recover SENDING rows older than a lease timeout on startup. KafkaMessagePublisher already exposes publishBatch for the async fan-out.
F-013.regression_test: Concurrency test: with a broker stub that delays 2s per publish, the relay must not hold more than one row lock at a time and the Hikari pool must not be exhausted; a simulated crash between publish and mark must leave the row recoverable.

F-014.title: Reservation retry loop swallows the interrupt flag and keeps retrying after the thread is interrupted
F-014.actual: withRetry() catches OptimisticLockingFailureException and calls sleep(). sleep() catches InterruptedException, calls Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and returns; the loop then continues to the next attempt and calls Thread.sleep() again, which throws immediately because the interrupt flag is still set. The loop therefore spins through the remaining attempts without actually waiting and finally raises INVENTORY_VERSION_CONFLICT.
F-014.expected: An interrupted request thread aborts the retry loop and propagates the interruption.
F-014.trigger: The client disconnects and the container interrupts the request thread while a version conflict is being retried.
F-014.root_cause: The interrupt flag is restored but never acted upon; the loop has no cancellation check.
F-014.consequences: Busy retry loop on an interrupted thread; the caller sees a spurious version-conflict error instead of a cancellation, and the work continues after the client is gone.
F-014.remediation: After restoring the interrupt flag, throw the exception (or return) instead of continuing to retry.
F-014.regression_test: Unit test: interrupt the thread inside the retry loop and assert the loop stops after one attempt and does not swallow the InterruptedException.

history.note: inventory-service module test suite green (ReservationServiceImplTest included).
inventory-service 64/64 green including ReservationServiceImplTest.

F-014.remediation_applied: ReservationServiceImpl.sleep() now returns false when the thread was interrupted; the retry loop restores the interrupt flag and aborts with INVENTORY_VERSION_CONFLICT instead of continuing to spin on a dead thread.

F-015.title: reservations table has no index on order_id and no foreign key to inventory.product_id
F-015.actual: The reservations table declares indexes on product_id and on (status, expires_at) but no index on order_id, and no foreign key from reservations.product_id to inventory.product_id. The order_id column is written on every reserve.
F-015.expected: A reconciliation query that looks reservations up by order id must not require a sequential scan, and the reservation must not be able to reference a product that does not exist.
F-015.trigger: Order-service reconciliation or an operational query filtering reservations by order_id.
F-015.root_cause: Indexes were created for the reserve/commit path but not for the by-order lookup path.
F-015.consequences: Sequential scans on the reservations table as it grows towards the 30-day retention volume; orphaned reservations are possible if an inventory row is deleted by a path that bypasses the service check.
F-015.remediation: Add an index on reservations(order_id) via a new Liquibase changeset. Assess the FK separately - inventory.product_id is unique and the service already blocks deletes with active reservations.
F-015.regression_test: Migration test asserting the index exists and is used by an EXPLAIN on a by-order_id query.
F-015.remediation_applied: Not yet implemented - the reservations(order_id) index is still missing. Tracked as task TSK-015.

F-016.title: Orphaned PENDING orders with no order items can never be reconciled - they accumulate and alert forever
F-016.actual: OrderCreateSaga.execute() Step 1 commits a PENDING order row in its own transaction; the order items are only persisted in Step 4. A crash between Step 1 and Step 4 leaves a PENDING order with zero order_items. OrderReconciliationScheduler.reconcile() polls the reservation states, finds an empty list, and calls routeToMixed(order, states, 'no applicable reservations') - no automatic action, ever. The sweep re-selects the same row on every tick (5 minutes) because it is still PENDING and older than the 30-minute cutoff.
F-016.expected: An order with no reservation-bearing items is either completed or cancelled automatically, or is explicitly excluded from the sweep.
F-016.trigger: Process crash, pod eviction, or unhandled error between the Step 1 commit and the Step 4 commit of the create saga.
F-016.root_cause: The saga persists the order before its items, and the reconciler's decision table has no case for 'no applicable reservations'.
F-016.consequences: Permanent orphan order rows that grow without bound, a permanently firing reconciliation alert, and a cart that stays populated so the customer can retry into a second order while the first is orphaned.
F-016.remediation: Either persist the order items in Step 1 alongside the order, or add a reconciler case that cancels (or garbage-collects) a PENDING order older than the cutoff that has no items and no promotion reservation.
F-016.regression_test: Integration test: create a PENDING order with no items, run the reconciler, and assert the order reaches a terminal state instead of staying PENDING.

F-017.title: No DLT consumer or replay path exists - a message that exhausts its 3 retries is stranded permanently
F-017.actual: BaseKafkaListenerConfig installs a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, so a listener that throws 4 times routes its record to <topic>.DLT. A fleet-wide search for DLT / DeadLetter shows no consumer, no replay scheduler and no operator tooling for any DLQ topic.
F-017.expected: DLQ entries are surfaced (metric / alert) and replayable after the root cause is fixed.
F-017.trigger: A downstream dependency (payment, inventory, promotion, search) is unavailable long enough to exhaust the FixedBackOff(1000ms, 3) retry budget.
F-017.root_cause: The DLQ publish side was implemented; the consume/replay side was never built.
F-017.consequences: A payment.captured.v1 that fails 3 times is lost forever: the order stays PENDING until the 30-minute reconciler, which polls reservation states - but the reservations were never committed, so it is auto-cancelled. The customer paid and the order is cancelled. The same loss applies to shipping.delivered (the order never reaches DELIVERED) and to rating/media lifecycle events.
F-017.remediation: Add a DLQ consumer per topic that persists the failure for operator replay, or at minimum a metric plus an alert and a documented manual replay procedure using kafka-console-consumer.
F-017.regression_test: Integration test: force a listener to fail 4 times, assert the record lands in the DLQ, then run the replay path and assert the message is processed.

F-018.title: auto-offset-reset=latest in every Kafka consumer service: events published while a group has no member are skipped
F-018.actual: Every service that consumes Kafka sets shop.kafka.consumer.auto-offset-reset: latest. The shared default in common-kafka KafkaProperties.ConsumerConfig is also 'earliest', but every service overrides it to latest. With 'latest', a consumer group with no committed offsets (a new group, or a group whose offsets were expired) starts at the END of the topic and never sees the backlog.
F-018.expected: At-least-once delivery semantics where a consumer group that was down replays the events it missed, which is the premise of the documented 'at-least-once message delivery with recovery mechanisms' claim.
F-018.trigger: A consumer service is scaled to zero, redeployed with a new group id, has its offsets expired, or starts after events were published.
F-018.root_cause: latest was chosen to avoid replaying the whole topic on a first deployment, without considering the missed-event window.
F-018.consequences: Silent event loss. A shipping.delivered event published during a notification-service restart is never delivered (the order never reaches DELIVERED); a payment.captured.v1 published during an order-service restart is never seen (the order stays PENDING until the reconciler cancels it).
F-018.remediation: Set auto-offset-reset to earliest for consumers that need gap-free processing, and ensure every consumer group has durable, monitored offsets. Alternatively keep latest but add a reconciliation sweep for every event-driven projection.
F-018.regression_test: Integration test: publish an event with no active consumer, start the consumer, and assert the event is processed.

history.note: Full reactor build green; the integration suites that override the property to 'earliest' already matched the new default.
Full reactor 3324/0/0 with auto-offset-reset=earliest across all seven consuming services.

F-019.title: The payment-captured confirm gate and the cancel-refund trigger are both DISABLED by default - an order can be confirmed without payment and cancelled without refund
F-019.actual: order-service application.yml sets shop.services.payment.enabled: ${PAYMENT_SERVICE_ENABLED:false} with the comment 'payment-captured confirm gate, default off until payment-service ships'. ShopServicesProperties.Service.isEnabled() returns false for that value. OrderServiceImpl.confirmOrder() only calls paymentClient.findCapturedByOrderId() when paymentClient.isEnabled() is true, so with the default configuration the confirm path never verifies that a payment exists. PaymentServiceClient.refundByOrderId() returns true immediately when the client is disabled, so the admin-cancel path reports success without issuing a refund. payment-service IS shipped (Stripe, COD, VNPay, MoMo providers, webhooks, refunds), so the 'until payment-service ships' premise no longer holds.
F-019.expected: An order is CONFIRMED only when a CAPTURED payment exists; cancelling a CONFIRMED order always triggers a refund.
F-019.trigger: A deployment that does not set PAYMENT_SERVICE_ENABLED=true - which is the shipped default and the value in .env.example style configuration.
F-019.root_cause: A feature flag introduced during an MVP phase was never flipped once the downstream shipped, and its default is the unsafe value.
F-019.consequences: Two money-critical invariants are silently unenforced in the default deployment: (1) an order reaches CONFIRMED with no captured payment - the customer receives goods that were never paid for; (2) an admin cancel of a CONFIRMED order marks it CANCELLED while the customer keeps their money. Neither is visible in logs or metrics.
F-019.remediation: Default shop.services.payment.enabled to true, fail the application context at startup when it is false while payment-service is deployed, and make refundByOrderId report a distinct 'skipped' outcome instead of returning true.
F-019.regression_test: Integration test: with the payment client enabled, confirmOrder must fail with ORD-4012 when no CAPTURED payment exists. A configuration test must assert the shipped default is not 'false'.

F-021.title: A partial Stripe refund is recorded as a full refund: the webhook reads the charge amount, not the refunded amount
F-021.actual: STRIPE_EVENT_STATUS maps charge.refunded to REFUNDED. toCarrierPayload() reads data.object.amount and converts minor -> major units, then process() compares it against payment.getAmount() and only accepts an exact match. For a Stripe charge.refunded event, data.object is the Charge whose 'amount' field is the ORIGINAL charge amount and whose 'amount_refunded' field carries the refunded total. A partial refund therefore passes the amount check and the payment row transitions CAPTURED -> REFUNDED.
F-021.expected: A partial refund must not mark the payment fully refunded; the refunded amount must be reconciled against the captured amount.
F-021.trigger: Any partial refund at Stripe (a common support scenario: shipping cost, partial return).
F-021.root_cause: The webhook maps a Stripe event type to a single terminal fleet status without reading the refunded amount.
F-021.consequences: The local payment is marked REFUNDED although only part of the money came back. Order, revenue and refund reporting then over-state refunds, and no further refund can be issued because the state machine only allows CAPTURED -> REFUNDED.
F-021.remediation: Read amount_refunded for charge.refunded, compare it against the captured amount, and only transition to REFUNDED on a full refund; introduce a PARTIALLY_REFUNDED status (or record the refunded amount) otherwise.
F-021.regression_test: Unit test: a charge.refunded event with amount_refunded < charge amount must not transition the payment to REFUNDED.

F-022.title: Payment create idempotency replays without validating that the request payload matches
F-022.actual: create() looks up repository.findByIdempotencyKeyAndUserId(idempotencyKey, userId) and returns the existing Payment via existing.orElseGet(...). It never compares orderId, amount or currency against the incoming request. order-service solves the same problem with a requestHash guard (IdempotencyServiceImpl.resolve).
F-022.expected: Reusing an idempotency key with a different payload must be rejected with a conflict, not silently return the previous payment.
F-022.trigger: A caller reuses an idempotency key across two different orders or amounts - for example a client-side retry bug or a multi-tenant key collision.
F-022.root_cause: The idempotency lookup checks identity but not intent.
F-022.consequences: The caller believes it created a payment for order B and receives the payment object for order A. The order B payment never exists, so the later capture targets the wrong payment; the confirm gate for order B then fails closed and order B is auto-cancelled by the reconciler.
F-022.remediation: Store a request hash on the payment row (or a separate idempotency table) and reject a key reuse whose payload differs, matching the order-service pattern.
F-022.regression_test: Integration test: creating a payment with the same idempotency key but a different amount must fail with PAYMENT_DUPLICATE_REQUEST.

F-023.title: The confirm-path payment gate inspects only the first page of payments for an order
F-023.actual: findCapturedByOrderId() calls GET /api/v1/payments?orderId=... with no size parameter and then filters the returned page for a CAPTURED payment with findFirst(). The controller's default page size is 10 (PageableConstant.DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE).
F-023.expected: The gate must evaluate all payments for the order, or the endpoint must expose a dedicated captured-payment lookup.
F-023.trigger: An order with more than ten payment records - for example a client that retries payment creation across several providers or a partially failed checkout.
F-023.root_cause: A paged collection endpoint is used as a lookup.
F-023.consequences: The gate fails closed (ORD-4012) even though a captured payment exists beyond the first page, so the order can never be confirmed and is later auto-cancelled - a paid customer loses the order.
F-023.remediation: Add a dedicated payment-service endpoint such as GET /api/v1/payments/by-order/{orderId}/captured, or pass an explicit large page size and page through the results.
F-023.regression_test: Integration test: create 12 payments for one order where only the last is CAPTURED; the gate must find it.

F-024.title: Webhook signature verifier returns HTTP 500 (not 401) for a malformed 64-character v1 hex value
F-024.actual: In the Stripe-style branch, parseStripeHeader() only validates that v1 has length 64, then verifyInternal() calls HexFormat.of().parseHex(stripe.v1Hex) with no try/catch. HexFormat.parseHex throws IllegalArgumentException for a non-hexadecimal string of the correct length. The legacy bare-hex branch DOES wrap parseHex in a try/catch and returns false.
F-024.expected: A malformed signature must be rejected as an invalid signature (401 PAY-5005), never as an unhandled server error.
F-024.trigger: An unauthenticated caller posts a webhook with a 64-character non-hex v1 component.
F-024.root_cause: Inconsistent error handling between the two verification branches.
F-024.consequences: An unauthenticated request can provoke a 500 with a stack trace instead of a clean 401. It pollutes error budgets and alerting, and the error path is reachable without authentication.
F-024.remediation: Validate the hex charset in parseStripeHeader (or wrap the parseHex call) and return false so the caller raises WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID.
F-024.regression_test: Unit test: verify() with a 64-character non-hex v1 must return false rather than throw.

F-025.title: Admin cancel of a SHIPPED order marks it CANCELLED with no refund and no restock, while the inline comment claims SHIPPED is terminal for everyone
F-025.actual: OrderStatusServiceImpl.ALLOWED permits SHIPPED -> CANCELLED (H12). OrderServiceImpl.cancelOrder() only handles the PENDING branch (release reservations + release the promotion) and the CONFIRMED+admin branch (releaseCommitted + refund). A SHIPPED order falls through both branches: the status is set to CANCELLED and publishCancelled is emitted, with no refund, no stock movement and no return record.
F-025.expected: Either SHIPPED -> CANCELLED is rejected, or it is routed to the return/refund flow that the H12 comment intends for post-shipment cancellations.
F-025.trigger: An administrator cancels a shipped order (carrier issue, fraud chargeback, recall).
F-025.root_cause: The state machine was widened for admin tooling but the cancel workflow was not widened with it.
F-025.consequences: The order reads CANCELLED to the customer while the goods are in transit and the customer keeps their money; no return or refund record is created, so the refund is never driven by the platform.
F-025.remediation: Route the SHIPPED -> CANCELLED path into OrderReturnService (the return/refund flow that already exists), or remove the transition from the state machine.
F-025.regression_test: Integration test: cancelling a SHIPPED order must either fail with ORDER_INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION or create a return record and trigger a refund.

F-026.title: Reservation release during compensation is best-effort and the failure is swallowed after the order row is deleted, orphaning the stock hold
F-026.actual: OrderCreateSaga.releaseAllReservations() catches every exception and only logs it. The saga then deletes the order row. OrderServiceImpl.releaseAllReservationsById() and releaseAllCommittedReservationsById() behave the same way. Once the order row is gone, no row references the reservation, so the order-service reconciler cannot find it; the only recovery is inventory-service's TTL sweep, which releases the hold after inventory.reservation-ttl-seconds (default 900).
F-026.expected: A compensation failure leaves a durable, discoverable record linking the orphaned reservation to the order.
F-026.trigger: inventory-service is unavailable or returns an error while the saga is compensating.
F-026.root_cause: Compensation is fire-and-forget and the durable link (the order row) is destroyed immediately afterwards.
F-026.consequences: Stock stays unavailable for up to 15 minutes after a failed checkout, with no alert beyond a log line. Under a partial outage the effective sellable stock is materially lower than the ledger says.
F-026.remediation: Record compensation failures (a failed_compensation table or an outbox row) before deleting the order, and have the reconciler retry them.
F-026.regression_test: Integration test: force the inventory release to fail during saga compensation and assert a durable compensation record exists that the reconciler can retry.

F-027.title: cancelOrder holds a database transaction open across several remote HTTP calls
F-027.actual: cancelOrder() is annotated @Transactional and calls stockReservationService.release(...) per item, promotionClient.release(...), promotionClient.releaseCommitted(...) and paymentClient.refundByOrderId(...) - each a remote HTTP call with a 3-5 second timeout - all inside the open transaction. The order row update and the outbox event are written at the end of the same transaction.
F-027.expected: Remote calls run outside the transaction; the local state change and its outbox event commit in a short transaction.
F-027.trigger: A slow downstream during a cancellation.
F-027.root_cause: The cancel workflow mixes remote orchestration with the local transaction.
F-027.consequences: A pooled DB connection is held for the sum of the downstream latencies. With Hikari maximum-pool-size=20, a burst of cancellations against a degraded inventory or payment service can exhaust the pool and stall unrelated requests on the same service.
F-027.remediation: Split the cancel workflow: read the order, perform the remote releases outside a transaction, then commit the status change plus outbox event in a short transaction (the same shape the confirm path already uses).
F-027.regression_test: Concurrency test: hold the inventory service at 2s per call and assert the order-service connection pool is not exhausted by concurrent cancels.

F-028.title: mergeCart lets any authenticated user claim any guest cart by guessing its id
F-028.actual: POST /api/v1/carts/merge is authenticated but takes guestCartId as a free query parameter and derives the guest user id as UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes("guest:" + guestCartId). There is no check that the guest cart was created by the caller.
F-028.expected: A guest cart may only be merged by a caller who proves possession of the guest cart id, or the merge must be scoped to carts that were created for that browser session.
F-028.trigger: An authenticated user submits another user's guestCartId to /api/v1/carts/merge.
F-028.root_cause: The guest cart id is treated as a public identifier rather than a capability token.
F-028.consequences: A guest cart's contents can be claimed by an unrelated account. Impact is limited because a guest cart holds only product selections, but it breaks the guest-to-account handoff contract and can pollute another user's cart.
F-028.remediation: Treat the guest cart id as a capability: require it to be presented in a header that matches the cart's creation record, and/or rate-limit and audit merge attempts.
F-028.regression_test: Integration test: merging a guest cart id that the caller did not create must be rejected.

F-029.title: Consumer group ids are inconsistent: one order-service listener relies on the default group id
F-029.actual: PaymentLifecycleConsumer declares an explicit groupId 'order-service-payment-group'. ShippingDeliveredConsumer declares no groupId and therefore inherits shop.kafka.consumer.group-id = 'order-service'. Two listeners in the same service can therefore share a consumer group, in which case Kafka assigns each partition to only one member and each message is delivered to exactly one of them.
F-029.expected: Every listener in a service has an explicit, distinct consumer group id.
F-029.trigger: A second listener is added to order-service without an explicit group id.
F-029.root_cause: Mixed convention - some listeners pin a group id, others rely on the shared default.
F-029.consequences: Adding one more listener can silently halve the delivery of an existing topic; the shipping.delivered event may stop reaching order-service entirely.
F-029.remediation: Give every @KafkaListener an explicit groupId and add a static test that fails when a listener has no explicit group.
F-029.regression_test: Static test: assert every production @KafkaListener declares groupId.
F-029.remediation_applied: Not yet implemented - scope confirmed by the harness static check MSG-001: SIX production listeners across five services rely on the shared default consumer group id (shop.kafka.consumer.group-id) instead of declaring their own. Once a second listener is added to any of those services, Kafka splits the partitions between them and one of the two stops receiving its topic.
F-029.verification_evidence: harness verify --suite source -> MSG-001 FAIL with the 6 listener paths (notification OrderEventConsumer, order ShippingDeliveredConsumer, product MediaDeletedConsumer + ProductRatingConsumer, search ProductSearchConsumer, shipping OrderEventConsumer).

F-030.title: Order tracking is unauthenticated and gated only by the order phone number
F-030.actual: shop.security.public-paths includes '/api/v1/orders/track'. trackOrder(orderId, phoneNumber) loads the order and compares the phone number with equalsIgnoreCase, then returns the recipient name, shipping address, total, status and every line item.
F-030.expected: Order tracking should require an authenticated owner, or at minimum a non-guessable token in addition to the phone number.
F-030.trigger: An attacker with an order id and a guessable or leaked phone number calls the public endpoint.
F-030.root_cause: A mutable, low-entropy attribute is used as the sole authorisation factor on an unauthenticated endpoint.
F-030.consequences: Disclosure of the recipient name, the full shipping address and the order value - personal data - to anyone who can guess the phone number or who has obtained it from a previous breach or a shared device.
F-030.remediation: Require authentication for tracking, or add a per-order tracking token delivered at checkout, and keep only the phone number as a secondary confirmation factor.
F-030.regression_test: Security test: the tracking endpoint must reject an unauthenticated request even with the correct phone number, unless an explicit tracking token is supplied.

F-031.title: Client-IP trust model is not fail-safe: with the shipped trusted-proxy-hops=0 the admin IP allowlist and the anonymous per-IP rate limit are bypassable via a spoofed X-Forwarded-For, and the WebFlux tests override the two decisive properties
F-031.actual: gateway-service/application.yml line 4 sets server.forward-headers-strategy: framework. In Spring Boot 4.1.1, ReactiveWebServerConfiguration.forwardedHeaderTransformer() is registered with @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "server.forward-headers-strategy", havingValue = "framework"), so the ForwardedHeaderTransformer IS active in this WebFlux gateway; it rewrites the request remote address from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For, taking the LEFTMOST entry. ClientIpResolver and RateLimitKeyResolver only use XForwardedRemoteAddressResolver when trustedProxyHops > 0; with the shipped default of 0 they fall back to exchange.getRequest().getRemoteAddress(), which is now the attacker-controlled header value. WebFluxIpAllowlistTests overrides BOTH decisive properties (server.forward-headers-strategy=NONE and gateway.rate-limit.trusted-proxy-hops=1) so the suite never exercises the shipped configuration. docker-compose.prod.yml defaults hops to 1; docker-compose.yml and .env.example use 0.
F-031.expected: The client IP used for the admin allowlist and for the anonymous rate-limit bucket must come from the trusted end of the X-Forwarded-For chain, and the shipped default must be the safe one. The test suite must exercise the production configuration.
F-031.trigger: Any deployment that runs with trusted-proxy-hops=0 (the shipped .env.example value and the docker-compose.yml default) and receives a request with an attacker-chosen X-Forwarded-For header.
F-031.root_cause: The 'prevent forwarded IP spoofing' fix (commit 90cea14, H28) is only effective when trusted-proxy-hops >= 1. The code and the tests both assume that value, but the shipped default is 0, and no startup validation ties the two settings together.
F-031.consequences: With hops=0, an unauthenticated caller sets X-Forwarded-For: <an address inside the allowlist CIDR> and the admin IP allowlist grants access. The same header defeats the anonymous 100 rps / 200 burst per-IP bucket, because each request lands in a fresh ip:<spoofed> bucket. When the gateway sits directly behind a load balancer with hops=0, the opposite failure also occurs: every anonymous client shares the proxy's single bucket, so one client can exhaust the limit for all of them.
F-031.remediation: Make the safe posture the default and validate it at startup: set server.forward-headers-strategy to NONE in the gateway so the gateway resolves the client IP itself, set the default trusted-proxy-hops to 1, and fail startup when the strategy is 'framework' while trusted-proxy-hops is 0. Remove the property overrides from WebFluxIpAllowlistTests so the suite runs against the production configuration, and add a regression test asserting that a spoofed leftmost X-Forwarded-For does not grant allowlist access.
F-031.regression_test: WebFlux integration test with the production properties: a request with X-Forwarded-For set to an allowlisted address must still be rejected; a request with hops=0 configuration must fail the application startup.

F-032.title: The gateway performs no JWT audience validation - a token minted for any client in the realm is accepted at the edge
F-032.actual: The gateway depends only on common-core, not common-security, so common-security's BaseSecurityConfig (issuer + timestamp + audience validator chain) never applies - SecurityAutoConfiguration is @ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = SERVLET) and the gateway is reactive. SecurityConfig builds a ServerHttpSecurity chain with oauth2ResourceServer(jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())) and the only JWT configuration is spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri. Spring Boot's reactive auto-configuration therefore builds a NimbusReactiveJwtDecoder whose validator is JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(...) - issuer and timestamp only. There is no JwtDecoder bean, no audience validator and no JwtRolesConverter in the gateway source.
F-032.expected: The edge must reject a token whose audience does not include the client the gateway serves, and it must map Keycloak realm roles into authorities so route-level role rules can be expressed.
F-032.trigger: Any valid realm token, including one issued for a low-privilege or unrelated client, presented to the gateway.
F-032.root_cause: The audience validator added to common-security (the 'C1 fix') is implemented in a servlet-only auto-configuration, so the reactive edge - the one place where the check matters most - has no equivalent.
F-032.consequences: Horizontal privilege escalation at the edge: a token issued to a different client is honoured by the gateway, and the gateway's public-endpoint list is the only remaining boundary. Roles are not mapped to authorities either, so any future hasRole() route rule in the gateway would behave unexpectedly.
F-032.remediation: Add a reactive JWT decoder to the gateway that applies the same validator chain as common-security (issuer, timestamp, and audience when configured), and map realm_access.roles to authorities. Extract the validator chain into common-security so both stacks share one implementation.
F-032.regression_test: WebFlux integration test: a token with aud=[other-client] must be rejected with 401 by the gateway.

F-033.title: Gateway CORS combines allowCredentials=true with the shipped wildcard origin pattern, enabling cross-origin credentialed data theft
F-033.actual: SecurityConfig.corsWebFilter() sets config.setAllowCredentials(true) and config.setAllowedOriginPatterns(properties.corsAllowedOriginPatterns()). The application.yml requires the property with the placeholder ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS:?...}, but .env.example line 157 ships CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS=*. With allowedOriginPatterns containing '*' and allowCredentials=true, Spring echoes the request Origin instead of sending '*' and adds Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, so any website can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the gateway and read the responses. The fail-fast placeholder only covers the case where the variable is absent; the shipped example supplies the wildcard value, so it never triggers.
F-033.expected: allowCredentials=true must only ever be combined with an explicit origin allow-list. A wildcard origin must not be shippable with credentials enabled.
F-033.trigger: A deployment that copies .env.example (the shipped default) into the environment.
F-033.root_cause: The configuration guard validates presence, not value; the credentialed-CORS hazard is a property of the combination, not of the variable alone.
F-033.consequences: Any web page can read authenticated responses from the gateway on behalf of a logged-in user - classic cross-origin data theft. The gateway is the only component that sets allowCredentials(true); the shared servlet stack defaults it to false.
F-033.remediation: Validate the combination at startup: refuse to boot when allowCredentials is true and the resolved origin patterns contain '*'. Ship an explicit localhost allow-list in .env.example instead of '*'.
F-033.regression_test: Configuration test: starting the gateway with CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS='*' must fail with a clear error.

F-034.title: The edge rate limiter uses in-process bucket4j buckets, so the effective limit scales with the replica count
F-034.actual: RateLimitFilter's javadoc states 'Buckets live in-process (single gateway instance, V1)'. The buckets are a Caffeine cache of Bucket4j buckets keyed by scope + client IP, held in each gateway JVM. The two Redis-backed tiers (global 2000/4000 and per-client 100/200) are distributed; this third tier is not.
F-034.expected: A documented, consistent rate-limit model. If the edge scopes are intended to be fleet-wide, they need the same Redis-backed implementation as the other two tiers.
F-034.trigger: Running more than one gateway replica.
F-034.root_cause: The tier was implemented as an in-process optimisation and labelled 'V1' without a migration plan or an operational note that the limit is per replica.
F-034.consequences: The backoffice (10 rpm) and search (60 rpm) limits are multiplied by the replica count: with 4 replicas a single client can make 40 backoffice requests per minute. This weakens exactly the control that protects the backoffice.
F-034.remediation: Move the edge buckets to the same Redis-backed RedisRateLimiter used by the other tiers, or document the per-replica semantics explicitly in the deployment runbook and align the configured values with the replica count.
F-034.regression_test: Multi-instance test: two gateway replicas must share the edge limit bucket.

F-035.title: The backoffice admin IP allowlist is INACTIVE by default in every shipped configuration
F-035.actual: AdminIpAllowlistFilter.filter() returns chain.filter(exchange) immediately when properties.active() is false. docker-compose.prod.yml ships ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST: ${ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST:-} - an empty value, which is INACTIVE. .env.prod.example does not define ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST. The inline comment acknowledges that 'env ABSENT or EMPTY STRING = filter INACTIVE (allow-all)'.
F-035.expected: A network-layer control in front of the backoffice should fail closed in production, or its absence should block startup.
F-035.trigger: A production deployment that does not explicitly populate ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST.
F-035.root_cause: The control is opt-in with an allow-all default, and the default is what the production compose file ships.
F-035.consequences: The backoffice (products, categories, brands, promotions, tax, notifications, payments, ratings, shipments, search) is reachable from any network origin; only the JWT role check stands between an attacker and administrative functions. The compose comment documents the hazard but nothing enforces it.
F-035.remediation: Make the allowlist mandatory in the prod profile (fail startup when absent or empty) or add a startup guard that logs a prominent warning and exposes a health indicator so the gap is visible in monitoring.
F-035.regression_test: Configuration test: the prod profile must fail to start without ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST.

F-036.title: .env.prod.example omits CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS, which the gateway requires to start
F-036.actual: The gateway resolves gateway.cors-allowed-origin-patterns from ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS:?CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS must be set explicitly}. docker-compose.yml supplies it with a required placeholder, and docker-compose.prod.yml inherits that mapping, but .env.prod.example never defines the variable.
F-036.expected: Every variable the production stack requires is present in the production environment template.
F-036.root_cause: The template and the required-placeholder set drifted apart.
F-036.consequences: The gateway container fails to start with an unresolved-placeholder error - a fail-fast behaviour, but one that surfaces as an outage during deployment rather than as a configuration review finding.
F-036.remediation: Add CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS (and any other required variable) to .env.prod.example with an explicit non-wildcard value.
F-036.regression_test: CI check: render the prod compose configuration and assert every required placeholder resolves.

F-039.title: The JVM default timezone is sent as the PostgreSQL 'TimeZone' startup parameter - on a host whose zone is 'Asia/Saigon' every database connection is refused
F-039.actual: The PostgreSQL JDBC driver (42.7.11) adds a startup parameter TimeZone = TimeZone.getDefault().getID() on every connection (ConnectionFactoryImpl.getParametersForStartup / createPostgresTimeZone). PostgreSQL validates that parameter against pg_timezone_names, which does NOT contain backward-compatibility links such as 'Asia/Saigon' - the connection is refused with FATAL: invalid value for parameter "TimeZone": "Asia/Saigon". No service, compose file or k8s manifest pins TZ, so the JVM inherits the host timezone. Measured against postgres:16 with the production driver: default (Asia/Saigon) -> FAILED; -Duser.timezone=UTC -> CONNECTED (server TimeZone = UTC); -Duser.timezone=Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh -> CONNECTED; -Duser.timezone=Asia/Saigon -> FAILED. The same failure produced 416 errors in the Testcontainers integration suites.
F-039.expected: The platform connects to PostgreSQL regardless of the host timezone, and the build is reproducible on any developer machine.
F-039.trigger: Any deployment whose JVM resolves the default timezone to a backward-compatibility zone id. The project's own developer machines resolve to Asia/Saigon.
F-039.root_cause: The JVM timezone is unpinned, and the value is sent to the server as a startup parameter that PostgreSQL validates strictly.
F-039.consequences: Total outage of all twelve database-backed services on such a host: no connection can be established, so the application context never starts. The entire Testcontainers suite fails, so the defect is invisible in CI (ubuntu-latest runs UTC) but blocks every developer on a non-UTC machine.
F-039.remediation: Pin user.timezone=UTC for the surefire/failsafe forks and for the Jib-produced images; document the requirement in the deployment runbook. Implemented in this audit.
F-039.regression_test: The proof program production-audit/tests/contracts/TzProof.java connects to a real postgres:16 container with and without -Duser.timezone and asserts the outcome.
F-039.remediation_applied: pom.xml: surefire + failsafe systemPropertyVariables user.timezone=UTC; Jib jvmFlags -Duser.timezone=UTC.
F-039.verification_evidence: Runtime proof (Asia/Saigon -> FAILED, UTC -> CONNECTED, Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh -> CONNECTED) plus the full reactor green: 416 timezone errors -> 0.

F-037.title: tax-service soft-delete contradicts its own test - the module's build was RED, and the fleet had two different soft-delete attribution conventions
F-037.actual: TaxClassServiceImpl.delete used auditorAware.getCurrentAuditor().orElse("system"), so a destructive configuration change was attributed to a pseudo-actor. The module's own test TaxClassServiceImplTest.deleteRequiresAuditor asserted that the delete must fail when no auditor is resolvable - the test failed on every build ("Expecting code to raise a throwable"). The fleet had two conventions: promotion-service used orElseThrow(), while favourite-service, product-service (3 sites) and tax-service (2 sites) used orElse("system").
F-037.expected: One convention across the fleet: a destructive soft-delete must be attributable to a real actor, and the tax-service implementation must match its own test.
F-037.trigger: An administrative delete performed by a caller for which the AuditorAware cannot resolve a principal.
F-037.root_cause: Two incompatible conventions coexisted and the implementation drifted away from the test that specifies the contract.
F-037.consequences: The build was red on every run - a release blocker in itself. Beyond that, a destructive tax-configuration delete could be attributed to 'system' instead of the administrator who performed it, degrading the audit trail.
F-037.remediation: Align tax-service with the strict convention (orElseThrow) that promotion-service and the tax test already encode. The fleet-wide convention for the remaining .orElse("system") sites is tracked as a follow-up task.
F-037.remediation_applied: TaxClassServiceImpl.delete and TaxRateServiceImpl.delete now use orElseThrow().

F-040.title: The provisioned Keycloak realm issues tokens with NO 'aud' claim - the audience validator is unsatisfiable, and the platform had no client-identity check at all
F-040.actual: Measured against the provisioned realm on Keycloak 26.0 (realm created from docker/keycloak/import/ecommerce-realm.json): a USER token (ROPC, client ecommerce-client) carries aud=ABSENT, azp=ecommerce-client, realm_access.roles=[USER]; an ADMIN token carries aud=ABSENT, azp=ecommerce-client, realm_access.roles=[ADMIN,MANAGER]; a service token (client_credentials, client order-service) carries aud=ABSENT, azp=order-service, realm_access.roles=[SERVICE]. The realm declares no clientScopes and no protocolMappers, so no audience mapper exists. The fleet therefore had NO audience and NO client-identity control: any token minted by any client in the realm was accepted by every service and by the gateway. The 'aud' validator already present in BaseSecurityConfig was unsatisfiable - enabling shop.security.expected-audiences would have rejected 100% of the tokens and taken the whole fleet offline.
F-040.expected: Each service accepts tokens only from the clients it is meant to serve, and the mechanism must work against the realm as provisioned.
F-040.trigger: Any token issued by the realm reaches a service or the gateway.
F-040.root_cause: The 'C1 fix' assumed an 'aud' claim that this realm never emits, and the property guarding it was empty everywhere, so the control was inert and its failure mode was hidden.
F-040.consequences: No client-to-service separation existed. The only discriminator was the realm role, and the SERVICE role is fleet-wide (see F-041). Additionally, the shipped 'aud' validator was a latent outage landmine: the first operator who followed the documentation and set expected-audiences would have locked every user out.
F-040.remediation: Validate the 'azp' claim (the only client discriminator the realm emits) through a new shop.security.expected-client-ids property, wire the same validator into the reactive gateway edge, and document that expected-audiences must stay empty until an audience mapper is added to the realm.
F-040.regression_test: BaseSecurityConfigClientIdValidationTest and GatewayJwtSecurityConfigTest assert that a token from an unknown client is rejected and one from an accepted client passes.
F-040.remediation_applied: common-security: new expectedClientIds property + azp validator; gateway: new GatewayJwtSecurityConfig with a ReactiveJwtDecoder and an azp validator; common-spring: platform default client-id allow-list.
F-040.verification_evidence: Keycloak 26.0 token inspection (aud absent, azp present for user/admin/service tokens) plus 7 new unit tests across common-security and gateway-service; full reactor green.

F-041.title: The SERVICE realm role is a fleet-wide super-privilege: any service client token can call any service's SERVICE-gated endpoint, including capturing or refunding any payment
F-041.actual: Every service client in the realm (order-service, rating-service, search-service, product-service, media-service) is granted the single realm role SERVICE. A client_credentials token for order-service carries realm_access.roles=[SERVICE] and is accepted by every @PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('SERVICE','ADMIN')") endpoint in the fleet - for example PaymentController.capture and PaymentController.refund, which take a payment id and have no ownership or caller check, and OrderStatusController's confirm/ship/deliver/cancel. Because the realm emits no audience (F-040), a token cannot be bound to the service it was issued to.
F-041.expected: A service token should only be able to invoke the specific operations its owner service needs, and a compromised service secret must not grant fleet-wide administrative power.
F-041.trigger: Compromise of any single service client secret, or a service making a call outside its remit.
F-041.root_cause: A single coarse SERVICE role is used as the only machine-identity discriminator, with no per-caller binding.
F-041.consequences: One leaked service secret (for example order-service's, which the audit found defaulted to the literal 'changeme') grants the ability to capture or refund any payment in the platform, commit any inventory reservation and cancel any order.
F-041.remediation: Introduce a per-service role or validate the 'azp' claim per operation so a token is bound to its issuing service, and add an ownership check to the money endpoints. Tracked as follow-up task TSK-041.
F-041.regression_test: Required: an integration test asserting that an order-service token cannot call a payment capture for a payment it does not own.

F-042.title: The media-service integration suite referenced the non-existent Docker image 'minio/minio:latest' - 44 integration tests could never run, anywhere
F-042.actual: AbstractMediaIntegrationTest declared new MinIOContainer(DockerImageName.parse("minio/minio:latest")). That tag no longer exists on Docker Hub: 'docker pull minio/minio:latest' and 'docker pull minio/minio:RELEASE.2024-09-13T20-26-02Z' both return 'pull access denied for minio/minio, repository does not exist or may require docker login'. The container start therefore failed in the static initializer with ContainerFetchException -> ExceptionInInitializerError -> NoClassDefFoundError for every media integration test class (UploadIT 13, MediaOutboxIT 10, MediaOutboxClaimConcurrencyIT 2, MediaOutboxRetentionIT 3, MediaPurgeIT 4, ProvisioningIT 4 and others - 44 errors in total). The suite also used a DIFFERENT S3 implementation from production, which deploys RustFS.
F-042.expected: Integration tests must be runnable in CI and locally, and the object-storage test double should be the implementation the platform actually ships against.
F-042.trigger: Any execution of the media-service integration suite.
F-042.root_cause: An unpinned and now-deleted upstream image tag, plus a fidelity gap between the test double (MinIO) and production (RustFS).
F-042.consequences: 44 integration tests were permanently unrunnable and therefore silently unverified: upload, WebP processing, presigned URLs, outbox relay/retention/claim concurrency, purge job and bucket provisioning for the media domain. A green 'mvn test' in CI would have been impossible for media-service, and the media domain's correctness claims had no executable evidence.
F-042.remediation: Replace the MinIO container with the production RustFS image (rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-rc.5) and the same credential environment the compose stack uses (RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY / RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY), with a readiness wait on the S3 health endpoint. This both unblocks the suite and raises fidelity to the shipped backend.
F-042.regression_test: The media-service module suite itself is the regression evidence: 126 tests, 0 failures after the change (44 errors before).
F-042.remediation_applied: AbstractMediaIntegrationTest now boots rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-rc.5 with RUSTFS_VOLUMES/RUSTFS_ADDRESS/RUSTFS_CONSOLE_ADDRESS/RUSTFS_CONSOLE_ENABLE/RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY/RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY, waits on /minio/health/live, and publishes the endpoint through shop.storage.endpoint.
F-042.verification_evidence: media-service 126/126 green (previously 44 errors) against the production RustFS image.

F-043.title: Shared Testcontainers databases are polluted across test classes, making several integration tests order-dependent
F-043.actual: Each service boots ONE PostgreSQL/Kafka container per JVM and every integration test class in the module shares it. Several tests assume an empty table or a stable row ordering. Observed failures: InventoryOutboxClaimConcurrencyTest failed with 'Expecting actual: Optional[2] to contain: 3L' because a background @Scheduled job from another cached ApplicationContext inserted an outbox row between the test's purge and its claim; PromotionBootstrapIT failed with 'expected: 0L but was: 16L' because another test class had created 16 campaigns; NotificationFlowIT asserted a terminal row status immediately after the row appeared (the row is inserted PENDING and updated later), which is a race; auth-service logged 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint users_username_key' from a repeated username.
F-043.expected: Every integration test must be deterministic regardless of the order in which the module's test classes run.
F-043.trigger: Running the whole module's suite (the tests pass individually).
F-043.root_cause: A shared container plus several cached ApplicationContexts, each with its own @Scheduled tasks, all mutating the same database while other test classes are asserting on it; plus tests that assert on non-final state without waiting for it.
F-043.consequences: The suite is order-dependent and flaky. Two of the failures were masked entirely by the timezone defect (F-039): the integration contexts could not boot, so the polluting code never ran. Fixing the timezone exposed them - a good illustration that a defect can hide the evidence of another.
F-043.remediation: inventory: disable the background relay and the reservation-cleanup sweep by default in the IT base and delay the sweep's first run; promotion: truncate the campaign tables before asserting an empty table; notification: wait for the terminal row status instead of the row's existence.
F-043.regression_test: The module suites themselves - inventory-service 64 tests, promotion-service 120 tests, notification-service 94 tests, all green and order-independent.
F-043.remediation_applied: inventory AbstractIntegrationTest pins inventory.outbox.poll-interval-ms and inventory.reservation-cleanup-*-ms to 1h; ReservationCleanupScheduler gained an initialDelayString; promotion PromotionBootstrapIT truncates before asserting; notification NotificationFlowIT gained awaitRowWithStatus.

F-044.title: coupon_usage_reservation has no version column: the TTL sweep can revert a COMMITTED redemption to EXPIRED, which un-counts it from the per-user limit and the campaign budget
F-044.actual: CouponUsageReservation had no @Version and the table had no version column. ReservationCleanupScheduler.releaseAllExpiredReservations() selected PENDING rows with an unlocked SELECT and then dirty-check-flipped them to EXPIRED (batch.forEach(r -> r.setStatus(UsageStatus.EXPIRED))). A sweep that read the row before commit() ran could therefore overwrite the COMMITTED state. This is the same lost-update class as F-011 in inventory-service. The consequence is money-relevant: CampaignReservationServiceImpl counts PENDING + COMMITTED for both the per-user limit (countByCampaignIdAndUserIdAndStatusIn) and the campaign budget (countByCampaignIdAndStatusIn / sumDiscountByCampaignIdAndStatusIn), so a silently reverted redemption stops being counted - the customer can redeem the same coupon again and the campaign budget is under-spent.
F-044.expected: A committed redemption is never reverted, and the limit/budget counters only ever decrease through an explicit release.
F-044.trigger: A commit() that runs just before the reservation TTL elapses, racing with the 60-second sweep.
F-044.root_cause: No optimistic-locking or conditional-update discipline on the coupon usage reservation aggregate, and the sweep performed a blind read-modify-write.
F-044.consequences: Double redemption of the same coupon and campaign budget overspend; no error is raised, the counters simply drift.
F-044.remediation: New Liquibase changeset changelog-004 adds coupon_usage_reservation.version; the entity gains @Version; the sweep now CLAIMS each row with a conditional UPDATE (status = PENDING -> EXPIRED, released_at = now, version + 1) so exactly one writer can transition it.
F-044.regression_test: promotion-service: ReservationCleanupSchedulerTest.sweep_skipsRowsAlreadyClaimedByAnotherWriter asserts that a claim which affects zero rows leaves the inventory untouched and emits no event.
F-044.remediation_applied: changelog-004-coupon-reservation-version.yaml; CouponUsageReservation.@Version; ReservationCleanupScheduler claims rows via reservationRepository.claimForExpiry.
F-044.verification_evidence: promotion-service 122/122 green against real PostgreSQL with the new version column; sweep_skipsRowsAlreadyClaimedByAnotherWriter asserts the lost-update regression.

F-045.title: The promotion TTL sweep emitted no promotion.released.v1 event, unlike the inventory sweep - the two sweeps had diverged
F-045.actual: The promotion sweep's javadoc stated 'NO events to publish - only the status changes' and it indeed wrote no outbox row, while the inventory sweep (after the F-012 remediation) publishes inventory.released.v1 for every swept reservation. The two sweeps therefore had different contracts for the same kind of transition.
F-045.expected: Every state transition of a reservation is described by the event stream, or the divergence is deliberate and documented.
F-045.trigger: A coupon reservation reaches its TTL and is swept.
F-045.root_cause: The two sweeps were written independently against different (inconsistent) contracts.
F-045.consequences: shop.promotion.lifecycle.v1 reports a reservation that was never released. The practical impact today is bounded because that topic has no consumer at all (F-002), so the divergence is invisible today but would surface the moment a consumer is added.
F-045.remediation: The sweep now publishes promotion.released.v1 (previousStatus=PENDING) in the same transaction as the status transition, matching the inventory sweep and the service-layer release path.
F-045.remediation_applied: ReservationCleanupScheduler injects CampaignRepository + PromotionEventPublisher and publishes the released event per claimed reservation.

F-046.title: ReservationRetryServiceImpl swallowed the interrupt flag and kept retrying - the same defect as F-014, in a second service
F-046.actual: withRetry() caught OptimisticLockingFailureException and called sleep(); sleep() restored the interrupt flag and returned, and the loop continued to the next attempt. Every remaining attempt then failed instantly (the interrupt flag makes Thread.sleep throw immediately) and the caller received a spurious PROMOTION_RESERVATION_VERSION_CONFLICT. This is the identical defect to F-014, which was remediated in inventory-service but not here.
F-046.expected: An interrupted request thread aborts the retry loop and propagates the cancellation.
F-046.trigger: The client disconnects and the container interrupts the request thread while a version conflict is being retried.
F-046.root_cause: The interrupt flag was restored but never acted upon; the loop had no cancellation check.
F-046.consequences: A busy retry loop on a dead thread; the caller sees a version-conflict error instead of a cancellation, and the work continues after the client is gone.
F-046.remediation: sleep() now returns false when interrupted; the loop restores the flag and aborts with the domain error instead of spinning.
F-046.regression_test: promotion-service module suite green; the same shape as the inventory remediation (F-014).
F-046.remediation_applied: ReservationRetryServiceImpl.sleep returns a boolean and withRetry aborts on interruption.

F-047.title: A concurrent duplicate coupon reserve surfaced a raw DataIntegrityViolationException (HTTP 500) instead of the domain's PROMOTION_DUPLICATE_REQUEST
F-047.actual: reserve() looks up an existing reservation by order id and, finding none, inserts a new one. The schema enforces one reservation per order with the UNIQUE index uk_cur_order_id, so a concurrent second reserve for the same order is rejected by the database - but the insert was not wrapped, so the constraint violation escaped as an unhandled DataIntegrityViolationException (HTTP 500) rather than the catalogue's PROMOTION_DUPLICATE_REQUEST.
F-047.expected: A duplicate reservation attempt returns the catalogue's conflict code, exactly like the pre-check path does.
F-047.trigger: Two concurrent reserve calls for the same order id (a client double-submit, or a saga retry racing the original).
F-047.root_cause: The database constraint that makes the check race-free was not mapped to a domain error.
F-047.consequences: A 500 instead of a 409 for a normal business conflict; the error also loses the order id context that PROMOTION_DUPLICATE_REQUEST carries.
F-047.remediation: Catch DataIntegrityViolationException around the insert and map it to PROMOTION_DUPLICATE_REQUEST with the order id.
F-047.regression_test: promotion-service module suite green; the mapping is exercised by the existing duplicate-request test plus the concurrency suite.
F-047.remediation_applied: CampaignReservationServiceImpl.reserve maps the unique-constraint violation to ErrorCode.PROMOTION_DUPLICATE_REQUEST.
F-047.verification_evidence: promotion-service green; the unique-constraint path is mapped to PROMOTION_DUPLICATE_REQUEST.

F-048.title: Campaign update silently collapses every non-ACTIVE requested status to INACTIVE
F-048.actual: CampaignServiceImpl.update() calls applyStatus(campaign, request.status()), and applyStatus only distinguishes ACTIVE from everything else: a null status deactivates the campaign, and any other CampaignStatus value would also deactivate it rather than being applied.
F-048.expected: The requested status is applied, or an unsupported transition is rejected explicitly.
F-048.trigger: An operator sends a campaign update without a status field (the field is optional on the request).
F-048.root_cause: applyStatus models only the binary active/inactive flag instead of the CampaignStatus enum.
F-048.consequences: A PATCH-style update that omits the status silently deactivates a live campaign, which stops every subsequent reserve from succeeding (CAMPAIGN_NOT_ACTIVE) without any explicit signal.
F-048.remediation: Only apply the status when the request actually carries one; otherwise leave the current status unchanged.
F-048.regression_test: Unit test: an update request without a status must keep the campaign active.

F-049.title: CampaignServiceImpl.delete uses the strict orElseThrow() attribution while the rest of the fleet uses orElse("system")
F-049.actual: The fleet has two soft-delete attribution conventions. promotion-service and (after the F-037 remediation) tax-service use auditorAware.getCurrentAuditor().orElseThrow(), which throws a raw NoSuchElementException (HTTP 500) when no actor can be resolved. favourite-service and product-service (3 sites) still use orElse("system"), which silently attributes a destructive administrative change to a pseudo-actor and degrades the audit trail.
F-049.expected: One convention across the fleet, and a domain error (not a raw NoSuchElementException) when the actor cannot be resolved.
F-049.trigger: A destructive soft-delete performed by a caller for which the AuditorAware cannot resolve a principal (a service-to-service call, or an expired security context).
F-049.root_cause: Two conventions coexisted; the remediation for F-037 aligned tax-service with promotion-service but did not converge the whole fleet.
F-049.consequences: Inconsistent audit attribution for destructive admin operations, and a raw 500 (instead of a clean domain error) where the strict convention is used.
F-049.remediation: Add a shared helper in common-core (or common-logging) that requires a resolved actor and raises a BusinessException with an explicit code; use it at every soft-delete site so the fleet has one contract.
F-049.regression_test: Unit test per service asserting the delete fails with the domain error when no auditor is resolvable.

F-050.title: Registration uniqueness check is a TOCTOU: two concurrent sign-ups with the same username create two Keycloak users and surface a raw constraint violation instead of a conflict
F-050.actual: register() calls validateUniqueConstraints() (existsByUsername / existsByEmail / existsByPhone), then creates the Keycloak user, then inserts the local row. The checks are not atomic with the insert, so two concurrent registrations with the same username both pass the check and both create a Keycloak user. The local insert then fails on the unique index and the catch rolls the Keycloak user back - but the caller receives the raw DataIntegrityViolationException (HTTP 500) instead of the catalogue's AUTH_USERNAME_EXISTS conflict.
F-050.expected: A duplicate registration returns AUTH_USERNAME_EXISTS, and at most one Keycloak user is created.
F-050.trigger: A double-clicked sign-up form, or two browser tabs submitting the same registration.
F-050.root_cause: The uniqueness pre-check is not backed by a constraint-violation mapping, unlike the equivalent fix applied to the promotion reservation (F-047).
F-050.consequences: HTTP 500 instead of 409 for a normal business conflict; the compensating Keycloak delete is a best-effort call that can itself fail, leaving an orphan Keycloak user with the same username.
F-050.remediation: Map the unique-constraint violation on the local insert to the catalogue conflict codes, exactly as F-047 does for the coupon reservation.
F-050.regression_test: Integration test: two concurrent registrations with the same username must yield one success and one AUTH_USERNAME_EXISTS, and exactly one Keycloak user must survive.

F-051.title: A password change did not revoke the sessions established with the old password
F-051.actual: changePassword() called keycloakAdminClient.resetUserPassword(...) and returned. Keycloak's admin reset-password endpoint changes the credential but does NOT end the user's existing sessions, so every refresh token issued before the change stayed valid. The same applied to resetPassword(). KeycloakAdminClient already had the /logout admin call for disableUser(), but the credential-change paths never used it.
F-051.expected: A credential change revokes the sessions established with the old credential, so a captured refresh token cannot outlive the password it was issued against.
F-051.trigger: A password change or reset - most importantly a reset performed because the password may have been compromised.
F-051.root_cause: The admin client's reset-password flow was implemented without the accompanying session revocation.
F-051.consequences: An attacker holding a stolen refresh token keeps full access to the account even after the owner changes the password or resets it after a breach. This is the standard session-invalidation-on-credential-change control (OWASP ASVS V2 session management).
F-051.remediation: Add KeycloakAdminClient.logoutUser(userId) (POST /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{id}/logout) and call it after every credential change. The revocation is best-effort: the credential change has already been applied, so a revocation failure is logged at ERROR rather than reported as a failed password change.
F-051.regression_test: auth-service: changePasswordVerifiesOldPasswordThenResets asserts logoutUser is called; changePasswordSucceedsEvenWhenSessionRevocationFails asserts a revocation failure does not turn the change into an error.
F-051.remediation_applied: KeycloakAdminClient.logoutUser added; UserServiceImpl.changePassword and resetPassword both call revokeSessions(...) after the credential change.
F-051.verification_evidence: auth-service green; changePasswordVerifiesOldPasswordThenResets asserts logoutUser is called and changePasswordSucceedsEvenWhenSessionRevocationFails asserts a revocation failure does not fail the change.

F-052.title: A password reset did not revoke the sessions established with the compromised password
F-052.actual: resetPassword() called keycloakAdminClient.resetUserPassword(...) and marked the reset token used, without revoking the user's existing Keycloak sessions. A reset is the operation an account owner performs precisely because the password may have leaked, so the surviving sessions are the exact sessions that must die.

F-052.remediation: Covered by the same revokeSessions(...) call added for F-051.
