F-053.title: The password reset token has no version column: a reset token can be redeemed twice concurrently
F-053.actual: PasswordResetToken has a 'used' flag but no @Version. resetPassword() loads the token with findByTokenHashAndUsedFalse, changes the Keycloak password, then sets used=true and saves. Two concurrent redemptions of the same token both read used=false and both change the password; the last writer wins and the first password is silently replaced.
F-053.expected: A reset token is single-use even under concurrent redemption.
F-053.trigger: A reset link is opened twice, or an attacker races the legitimate owner.
F-053.root_cause: The consume step is a read-modify-write without a version guard or a conditional UPDATE.
F-053.consequences: The token can be used twice; the second use overwrites the password the owner just set, so the owner's chosen password is lost without any error.
F-053.remediation: Consume the token with a conditional UPDATE (UPDATE ... SET used = true WHERE token_hash = ? AND used = false) and only proceed when it affected one row; add a version column for the same reason as F-011 / F-044.
F-053.regression_test: Concurrency test: two concurrent redemptions of the same token must produce exactly one password change and one rejection.

F-054.title: The password reset email is never sent - the only PasswordResetEmailSender implementation logs instead of dispatching, so the reset flow cannot complete
F-054.actual: PasswordResetEmailSender is a port with exactly one implementation, DefaultPasswordResetEmailSender, whose sendResetEmail() body is a log.info line. forgotPassword() persists a reset token, calls the sender and reports success - so the API answers 'a password reset instruction has been sent' while no message ever leaves the process. The raw token is correctly NOT logged, so there is no leak; the flow is simply non-functional.
F-054.expected: The reset token reaches the user over the notification channel (notification-service already has an SMTP sender).
F-054.trigger: Any forgot-password request in a real deployment.
F-054.root_cause: The seam was created but no SMTP-backed implementation was wired.
F-054.consequences: Users cannot recover a forgotten password; the endpoint reports success, so the failure is invisible to operators and to the caller. Support load is the only signal.
F-054.remediation: Implement the sender on top of notification-service's SMTP channel (or a JavaMailSender), and fail the endpoint when the dispatch fails so the caller is not told a message was sent when it was not.
F-054.regression_test: Integration test: forgot-password must invoke a sender that records the delivery, and the reset link must work end to end.

F-055.title: A self-registration naming only privileged roles created an account with ZERO realm roles - the user could sign in but every authorization rule failed
F-055.actual: extractRoles() returned the USER fallback only when the request omitted the roles field entirely. When the request named a non-allowed role ({"ADMIN"}, {"ADMIN","SERVICE","MANAGER"}, ...) the whitelist filter removed every entry and the resulting EMPTY list was used for BOTH the Keycloak role assignment (createUser) and the local user_role rows. The pre-existing test registerAllDisallowedRolesResultsInEmptyList ASSERTED this behaviour, so the defect was locked in by its own specification.
F-055.expected: The whitelist exists to stop a self-registration obtaining a privileged role - not to strip the customer of their base role. A registration must always end up with at least USER.
F-055.trigger: A client that sends a roles field containing only privileged names (the field is deprecated but still accepted and bound).
F-055.root_cause: The fallback was applied to the pre-filter list instead of the post-filter list.
F-055.consequences: The account is created in Keycloak with no realm role and in the local database with no role row. The customer can authenticate, but every @PreAuthorize rule fails, and every @PreAuthorize-based endpoint returns 403 for an account that the registration flow reported as created. Recovering it requires an operator.
F-055.remediation: Apply the USER fallback to the POST-filter list, so an empty filtered result falls back to USER. The test was updated to assert the corrected behaviour (and renamed accordingly).
F-055.regression_test: auth-service: registerAllDisallowedRolesFallsBackToUser asserts Keycloak receives ["USER"] and the local DB receives the USER role row, and that the empty-role call never happens.
F-055.remediation_applied: UserServiceImpl.extractRoles now falls back to USER when the whitelist filter empties the list.
F-055.verification_evidence: auth-service green; registerAllDisallowedRolesFallsBackToUser asserts Keycloak receives ["USER"] and the local DB receives the USER role row.

F-056.title: The local role catalogue (USER, PM, ADMIN) does not match the provisioned Keycloak realm roles (ADMIN, USER, MANAGER, SERVICE)
F-056.actual: RoleName declares USER, PM and ADMIN, while the Keycloak realm ships ADMIN, USER, MANAGER and SERVICE. RoleMapper.toRoleName maps an unknown name to BusinessException.badRequest("auth.unsupported.role"), so the mismatch is handled cleanly at the API boundary - assigning MANAGER or SERVICE through /api/v1/roles returns a 400 with a clear code rather than an unmapped exception. The local catalogue is nevertheless a subset with one invented role (PM) that does not exist in the realm.
F-056.expected: The local role catalogue and the realm's realm roles stay in step.
F-056.trigger: An operator tries to grant MANAGER or SERVICE through the admin role API.
F-056.root_cause: The catalogue was written independently of the realm import.
F-056.consequences: The SERVICE role - which every service-to-service call depends on - cannot be managed through the auth-service admin API; MANAGER cannot be granted either. The mismatch is fail-closed (400) rather than dangerous.
F-056.remediation: Align RoleName with the realm (add MANAGER and SERVICE, or drop PM), or generate the catalogue from the realm at startup.
F-056.regression_test: Contract test asserting that every RoleName constant exists as a realm role in docker/keycloak/import/ecommerce-realm.json.

F-057.title: forgotPassword logs the email address of a non-existent account
F-057.actual: forgotPassword() returns the same generic message for every input (no user enumeration through the API - that part is correct), but it logs 'Password reset requested for non-existent email: {}' with the submitted address, while the existing-account branch logs the username. The log therefore becomes a list of addresses that do not belong to the platform.
F-057.expected: Logs do not accumulate third-party email addresses. A single indistinguishable log line per request is enough to drive an operational alert.
F-057.trigger: Any forgot-password request for an address that is not registered.
F-057.root_cause: The two branches log at different granularity.
F-057.consequences: The log stream becomes a soft user-enumeration oracle for anyone with log access, and it accumulates personal data about unrelated people.
F-057.remediation: Log one indistinguishable line per request (optionally with a hash of the address) and raise a counter for the not-found case so an enumeration attempt is still visible to monitoring.
F-057.regression_test: Unit test: the two branches produce the same log shape (no raw address for the not-found case).

F-058.title: product-service's outbox relay burned the whole retry budget inside one tick and then parked the event as FAILED, permanently losing the product lifecycle event
F-058.actual: Unlike the inventory, promotion and media relays, product-service's OutboxRelay returned TRUE from its publish-failure branch and kept draining the batch. Because the claim always takes the MIN(id) PENDING row, the next iteration re-claimed the SAME failing row and retried it, so the max-retries budget (10) was consumed within ONE tick instead of across the 5-second poll interval. The row was then parked as FAILED - and product-service has no retry, alert or repair path for FAILED rows - so a transient broker outage permanently lost the product lifecycle event. shop.product.lifecycle.v1 therefore stopped reaching search-service and the search index diverged from the catalogue with no repair route. Each retry also re-held the PESSIMISTIC_WRITE row lock across a blocking publish (compounding F-013).
F-058.expected: A publish failure leaves the row PENDING for the next tick, the retry budget is spread across ticks, and per-aggregate event ordering is preserved.
F-058.trigger: Any transient Kafka outage or broker error while the relay is draining.
F-058.root_cause: The relay's failure branch did not stop the batch, unlike every sibling relay.
F-058.consequences: Permanent, silent loss of product lifecycle events; the Elasticsearch index diverges from the catalogue with no automated repair.
F-058.remediation: The failure branch now returns FALSE (STOP), matching the inventory, promotion and media relays: the row stays PENDING, the retry budget is spread across ticks and ordering is preserved.
F-058.regression_test: product-service outbox relay test asserting that a failed publish leaves the row PENDING and stops the batch for that tick.
F-058.remediation_applied: product-service OutboxRelay publish-failure branch returns Boolean.FALSE (STOP) instead of Boolean.TRUE.
F-058.verification_evidence: product-service green; the relay failure branch now returns FALSE (STOP) so the row stays PENDING for the next tick.

F-059.title: product-service and rating-service had no outbox retention scheduler - their outbox tables grew without bound
F-059.actual: A fleet-wide scan for a retention scheduler showed inventory, promotion, media, payment, shipping and order all purge SENT outbox rows older than seven days; product-service and rating-service did not. product-service's repository did not even have the delete method, and rating-service HAD the method but no scheduler ever called it. Their outbox_events tables therefore grew by one row per domain mutation forever.
F-059.expected: Every event-producing service reclaims the space its outbox consumes.
F-059.root_cause: The retention job was added service by service and two were missed.
F-059.consequences: Unbounded table growth in two services - storage cost, ever-growing indexes, and slower claim queries (the claim does a MIN(id) sub-select over the PENDING set).
F-059.remediation: Added an OutboxRetentionScheduler to product-service (plus the missing repository delete method) and to rating-service (which already had the method). Only SENT rows are purged; PENDING, FAILED and DEAD rows are left for the relay and for operators.
F-059.regression_test: Integration test: after the retention job runs, SENT rows older than the window are gone while PENDING and FAILED rows remain.
F-059.remediation_applied: New OutboxRetentionScheduler in product-service and rating-service; deleteByStatusAndSentAtBefore added to product-service's repository.
F-059.verification_evidence: product-service and rating-service green with the new OutboxRetentionScheduler beans.

F-060.title: product-service soft-deletes a product without checking for active inventory reservations, while inventory-service refuses to delete an in-use inventory row
F-060.actual: InventoryServiceImpl.delete() refuses to delete an inventory row that has PENDING or COMMITTED reservations (ErrorCode.INVENTORY_IN_USE). The symmetric guard does not exist on the other side of the relationship: ProductServiceImpl.delete() soft-deletes the product unconditionally, so a product can be removed from the catalogue while stock for it is reserved or committed. The inventory row survives with a reference to a soft-deleted product.
F-060.expected: A product with live reservations cannot be removed from the catalogue, or the inventory row is released/compensated as part of the deletion.
F-060.trigger: An administrator deletes a product that a customer is currently checking out.
F-060.root_cause: The guard lives only on the inventory side, and inventory-service has no visibility of the product catalogue - the check would have to be an HTTP call, which the product-service does not make.
F-060.consequences: An orphaned inventory row for a deleted product; the checkout can still commit a reservation for a product that no longer exists; the reserved stock is never returned to the sellable pool.
F-060.remediation: Add a reference check to the product delete path (the same internal client pattern media-service already uses via MediaReferenceChecker / ProductMediaReferenceChecker), and make the check fail-safe: treat an unavailable reference service as 'referenced' so a delete is not performed on incomplete data.
F-060.regression_test: Integration test: deleting a product that has an active reservation must be rejected; deleting one with none must succeed.

F-061.title: product-service soft-deletes a variant with a hard-coded 'system' actor and without a stock check
F-061.actual: ProductVariantServiceImpl.delete() calls variant.markDeleted("system") - the actor is a literal, not the resolved principal, so a destructive administrative change is attributed to a pseudo-actor regardless of who performed it. It also performs no stock check, unlike the product delete path's sibling in inventory-service.
F-061.expected: The resolved actor is recorded, and a variant with live stock is not silently removed.
F-061.trigger: An administrator deletes a product variant.
F-061.root_cause: The variant delete path was written separately from the product/brand/category delete paths and hard-codes the actor.
F-061.consequences: The audit trail cannot attribute a variant deletion. Combined with F-049 (two conventions across the fleet) the soft-delete attribution is inconsistent in three different ways.
F-061.remediation: Resolve the actor through the same AuditorAware-based helper the fleet should share (see F-049), and add a stock-reference check.
F-061.regression_test: Unit test: the deleted variant records the authenticated actor.

F-062.title: The media upload path amplifies memory to hundreds of megabytes for a single maximum-size image
F-062.actual: The upload path holds, simultaneously: the raw source bytes (file.getBytes(), up to shop.media.max-upload-bytes), a decoded BufferedImage (width x height x 4 bytes - the guard permits up to 8192 x 8192, i.e. 268 MB for one image), and the encoded bytes of every rendered variant (up to six byte arrays). The source is also parsed twice: once by ImageMetadataReader for the EXIF/GPS inspection and once by ImageIO, and the image is decoded a second time by ImageIO.read after the dimension probe. The dimension guard limits width and height but the pixel-count guard is width*height <= 8192*8192, which is exactly the 268 MB case.
F-062.expected: The upload path must bound its peak heap so a single upload cannot exhaust the service's heap, and must not decode the same image twice.
F-062.trigger: An administrator uploads a large (but permitted) image.
F-062.root_cause: The size guard is expressed in source bytes and in pixel dimensions, but not in the memory the decoder will actually allocate; the header probe and the full decode are two separate passes over the same bytes.
F-062.consequences: A single upload can allocate several hundred megabytes of heap. Concurrent uploads multiply that, and the result is a heap-exhaustion outage of media-service rather than a rejected upload. The objective's 'memory and CPU behaviour for large uploads' requirement is not met.
F-062.remediation: Express the guard in decoded-memory terms (width x height x 4 plus the source size must fit a configured budget), decode once (reuse the ImageReader stream for both the dimension probe and the decode), and stream the source to the digest instead of materialising it twice.
F-062.regression_test: Performance test: upload an image at the configured maximum and assert the peak heap stays inside the configured budget; a unit test asserts that an image whose decoded size exceeds the budget is rejected before any large allocation.

F-063.title: Deleting a media asset does not check whether a live product still references it
F-063.actual: media-service already has the reference checker (ProductMediaReferenceChecker) and it is deliberately fail-safe - an unavailable reference service is treated as REFERENCED so the purge job skips the media. The DELETE endpoint path does NOT use it: MediaLifecycleServiceImpl.softDelete() soft-deletes unconditionally, so an administrator can remove a media asset that a live product still points at, leaving the product with a dangling image reference.
F-063.expected: Deleting a referenced media asset is refused (or the references are cleared first), with the same fail-safe posture the purge job uses.
F-063.trigger: An administrator deletes a media asset used by a live product.
F-063.root_cause: The reference check was wired into the background purge path but not into the interactive delete path.
F-063.consequences: A live product loses its image; the reference count and the catalogue disagree.
F-063.remediation: Apply the existing reference checker in the delete path, reusing the fail-safe semantics already implemented.
F-063.regression_test: Integration test: deleting a referenced media asset must be refused; deleting an unreferenced one must succeed.

F-064.title: The 'six WebP variants' claim is inaccurate: the renderer produces six objects for a JPEG/PNG upload, but only three of them are WebP
F-064.actual: VariantRenderer.render() walks the three variants (original, display, thumb) and, for each, emits the source format plus a WebP copy - unless the source format is already WebP. A JPEG upload therefore yields six objects (original.jpg, original.webp, display.jpg, display.webp, thumb.jpg, thumb.webp) of which THREE are WebP; a WebP upload yields three objects, all WebP.
F-064.expected: The documentation states the actual number of WebP variants per upload.
F-064.trigger: Any statement about how many WebP variants the platform produces.
F-064.root_cause: The documented count conflated 'variants' with 'WebP variants'.
F-064.consequences: A capacity or storage estimate based on the claim is wrong by a factor of two; an operator verifying the claim by counting WebP objects finds three, not six.
F-064.remediation: Correct the claim to 'three variants (original, display, thumb), each stored in the source format and in WebP - six objects for a JPEG or PNG upload, three for a WebP upload'.
F-064.regression_test: Integration test asserting the rendered object count per source format.

F-065.title: Hiding the only visible rating of a product crashed the moderation transaction - the administrator could not remove the review
F-065.actual: RatingEventService.record() reads the aggregate with findAggregateByProductId, whose JPQL averages over hidden = false AND deleted = false. When the last visible rating of a product is hidden, PostgreSQL returns a NULL average. toBigDecimal() called String.valueOf(raw), which for a null Object returns the literal string "null" (not null), and new BigDecimal("null") throws NumberFormatException. The exception propagated out of record(), inside the hide transaction, so the whole hide rolled back and the API answered 500. A moderator therefore could not remove the only review of a product - exactly the situation moderation exists for, and a dead end that leaves an abusive review visible.
F-065.expected: Hiding the last visible rating succeeds and reports an average of zero.
F-065.trigger: An administrator hides a rating when it is the only visible rating for its product.
F-065.root_cause: A NULL aggregate value was passed to a numeric parser that handled the 'not a BigDecimal' case but not the 'null' case.
F-065.consequences: The moderation endpoint fails with a 500 for a legitimate and important operation; the abusive review stays visible and the operator has no other route.
F-065.remediation: toBigDecimal() now maps a null aggregate to BigDecimal.ZERO.
F-065.regression_test: rating-service: RatingEventServiceTest.record_withNullAggregateAverage_writesZeroAverageInsteadOfFailing asserts the event is written with avgRating 0.00 and ratingCount 0.
F-065.verification_evidence: rating-service green; RatingEventServiceTest.record_withNullAggregateAverage_writesZeroAverageInsteadOfFailing asserts the event is written with avgRating 0.00 and ratingCount 0.

history.note: rating-service module green with the new regression test.
rating-service green; RatingEventServiceTest.record_withNullAggregateAverage_writesZeroAverageInsteadOfFailing asserts the event is written with avgRating 0.00 and ratingCount 0.

F-066.title: Remote calls are made inside database transactions in three more services (product media check, rating eligibility, order cancel)
F-066.actual: ProductServiceImpl.create/update call assertMediaExists -> mediaHeadClient.exists() inside the @Transactional method. RatingServiceImpl.submit calls eligibilityClient.isEligible() inside its @Transactional method. OrderServiceImpl.cancelOrder (already recorded as F-027) performs the inventory, promotion and payment calls inside its @Transactional method. Each holds a pooled DB connection and an open transaction for the duration of a remote round-trip (3-5 second timeouts).
F-066.expected: Remote calls run outside the transaction; the local state change commits in a short transaction - the shape the checkout saga already uses deliberately.
F-066.trigger: Any slowdown of media-service, order-service or the payment provider.
F-066.root_cause: The same pattern as F-027, repeated in three services that were written independently.
F-066.consequences: A degraded downstream holds DB connections and transactions open. With Hikari maximum-pool-size=20 a burst of concurrent requests against a slow dependency can exhaust the pool and stall unrelated requests on the same service.
F-066.remediation: Move the remote verification out of the transaction: perform it first, then open the short transaction for the write. Where the remote result must be authoritative (the rating eligibility check), fail the request rather than holding the transaction open.
F-066.regression_test: Concurrency test: hold the downstream at 2s per call and assert the service's connection pool is not exhausted.

F-067.title: The GHN and GHTK carrier adapters never contact the carrier - they fabricate a deterministic tracking number from the order id and leave the API token unused
F-067.actual: GhnCarrierAdapter holds an apiToken and a shopId and never uses either. createShipment() derives the tracking number locally: "GHN" + orderId.toString().replace("-","").substring(0,10).toUpperCase() (GHTK uses 9 characters and a dot separator). No HTTP call is made to the carrier. The ManualCarrierAdapter returns a null tracking number and the NoopCarrierAdapter returns "NOOP-<orderId>" and starts at PICKED_UP.
F-067.expected: Selecting a real carrier must create a real shipment with the carrier and record the carrier-issued tracking number.
F-067.root_cause: The carrier integrations were stubbed with a local derivation and the credential fields were left in place, so the configuration looks live.
F-067.consequences: No parcel ever reaches the carrier, so the customer receives a tracking number that the carrier does not know and that the carrier webhook can never confirm. The tracking number is also derived from the order id, so it is predictable, and two order ids sharing a 10-hex-character prefix would collide on the (unique) tracking-number column. The reconciliation scheduler then auto-delivers these phantom shipments after seven days and publishes shipping.delivered.v1, so the order is marked DELIVERED for a parcel that was never shipped.
F-067.remediation: Implement the real carrier API calls (create-shipment) and store the carrier-issued tracking number; until then make the adapters fail fast rather than fabricate a tracking number, and label them clearly as simulators.
F-067.regression_test: Contract test with a stubbed carrier endpoint asserting that the adapter calls the carrier and stores the returned tracking number; a unit test asserting the simulator adapters cannot be selected in a production profile.

F-068.title: A shipment that the carrier never confirmed is auto-delivered after seven days and drives the order to DELIVERED
F-068.actual: ReconciliationScheduler runs hourly and moves any shipment whose status is in-flight (PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY) and whose last carrier update is older than shop.shipping.auto-deliver-days (default 7) to DELIVERED with autoDelivered=true, publishing shipping.delivered.v1. The order-service consumes that event and marks the order DELIVERED. The rule does not distinguish a shipment the carrier confirmed from one that was never handed over (see F-067), and the carrier-seen timestamp is only written when a carrier webhook arrives - so a shipment that never reached the carrier is auto-delivered exactly like one whose tracking stalled.
F-068.expected: The auto-delivery rule should apply to shipments the carrier has acknowledged and then stopped updating, not to shipments that were never registered with the carrier.
F-068.trigger: A shipment stays in flight for seven days without a carrier update.
F-068.root_cause: The reconciliation rule uses only the last carrier update timestamp, with no evidence that the carrier ever accepted the parcel.
F-068.consequences: Orders reach DELIVERED without a delivery; the customer is told the parcel arrived. With F-067 (no real carrier call) this is the normal outcome for every GHN/GHTK shipment.
F-068.remediation: Record a carrier-acknowledged flag/timestamp when the carrier confirms the shipment, and restrict the auto-delivery rule to shipments the carrier has acknowledged.
F-068.regression_test: Integration test: a shipment never acknowledged by the carrier must not be auto-delivered.

F-069.title: The admin IP allowlist uses a prefix match without a path boundary, so a path that merely starts with a public prefix bypasses it
F-069.actual: isPublicStorefront() tests path.startsWith("/api/v1/products"), ("/api/v1/categories"), ("/api/v1/brands"), ("/api/v1/search"), ("/api/v1/ratings"), ("/api/v1/medias") and ("/api/v1/auth") with no trailing separator, and the webhooks bypass uses startsWith("/api/v1/webhooks/"). A request for a path such as /api/v1/ratings-admin or /api/v1/auth-internal therefore bypasses the allowlist even though it is not a public storefront route.
F-069.expected: The bypass must match a path segment boundary, exactly as the scope matching in RateLimitFilter already does (matchesPrefix compares against prefix or prefix + "/").
F-069.trigger: A request to a path whose name merely starts with a public prefix.
F-069.root_cause: A raw startsWith is used where the sibling filter already implements a segment-aware match.
F-069.consequences: Any route whose path begins with a public prefix is reachable from outside the allowlist. Today no such route exists, so the impact is latent - but it is exactly the kind of prefix confusion that becomes an allowlist bypass when a route is added.
F-069.remediation: Reuse the segment-aware prefix match that RateLimitFilter already implements.
F-069.regression_test: Unit test: a path such as /api/v1/ratings-admin must NOT be treated as a public storefront path.
